Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Understanding customer personality and behavior is pivotal for businesses to enhance customer satisfaction and increase revenue. Segmentation based on a customer's personality, demographics, and purchasing behavior allows companies to create tailored marketing campaigns, improve customer retention, and optimize product offerings.

A leading retail company with a rapidly growing customer base seeks to gain deeper insights into their customers' profiles. The company recognizes that understanding customer personalities, lifestyles, and purchasing habits can unlock significant opportunities for personalizing marketing strategies and creating loyalty programs. These insights can help address critical business challenges, such as improving the effectiveness of marketing campaigns, identifying high-value customer groups, and fostering long-term relationships with customers.

With the competition intensifying in the retail space, moving away from generic strategies to more targeted and personalized approaches is essential for sustaining a competitive edge.

Objective¶

In an effort to optimize marketing efficiency and enhance customer experience, the company has embarked on a mission to identify distinct customer segments. By understanding the characteristics, preferences, and behaviors of each group, the company aims to:

  1. Develop personalized marketing campaigns to increase conversion rates.
  2. Create effective retention strategies for high-value customers.
  3. Optimize resource allocation, such as inventory management, pricing strategies, and store layouts.

As a data scientist tasked with this project, your responsibility is to analyze the given customer data, apply machine learning techniques to segment the customer base, and provide actionable insights into the characteristics of each segment.

Data Dictionary¶

The dataset includes historical data on customer demographics, personality traits, and purchasing behaviors. Key attributes are:

  1. Customer Information

    • ID: Unique identifier for each customer.
    • Year_Birth: Customer's year of birth.
    • Education: Education level of the customer.
    • Marital_Status: Marital status of the customer.
    • Income: Yearly household income (in dollars).
    • Kidhome: Number of children in the household.
    • Teenhome: Number of teenagers in the household.
    • Dt_Customer: Date when the customer enrolled with the company.
    • Recency: Number of days since the customer’s last purchase.
    • Complain: Whether the customer complained in the last 2 years (1 for yes, 0 for no).

  2. Spending Information (Last 2 Years)

    • MntWines: Amount spent on wine.
    • MntFruits: Amount spent on fruits.
    • MntMeatProducts: Amount spent on meat.
    • MntFishProducts: Amount spent on fish.
    • MntSweetProducts: Amount spent on sweets.
    • MntGoldProds: Amount spent on gold products.

  3. Purchase and Campaign Interaction

    • NumDealsPurchases: Number of purchases made using a discount.
    • AcceptedCmp1: Response to the 1st campaign (1 for yes, 0 for no).
    • AcceptedCmp2: Response to the 2nd campaign (1 for yes, 0 for no).
    • AcceptedCmp3: Response to the 3rd campaign (1 for yes, 0 for no).
    • AcceptedCmp4: Response to the 4th campaign (1 for yes, 0 for no).
    • AcceptedCmp5: Response to the 5th campaign (1 for yes, 0 for no).
    • Response: Response to the last campaign (1 for yes, 0 for no).

  4. Shopping Behavior

    • NumWebPurchases: Number of purchases made through the company’s website.
    • NumCatalogPurchases: Number of purchases made using catalogs.
    • NumStorePurchases: Number of purchases made directly in stores.
    • NumWebVisitsMonth: Number of visits to the company’s website in the last month.

Since this project is about exploring customer personality and segmentation, some columns in the dataset don’t add value for analysis because they are either just identifiers or contain constant values:

  • ID – Only a unique code for each customer; doesn’t help in finding patterns.
  • Z_CostContact – Likely the same number for all rows (constant).
  • Z_Revenue – Often the same for everyone in this dataset.
  • t_Customer – Can be removed unless we plan to calculate how long a person has been a customer

These columns can be dropped to make the dataset cleaner and focus on the variables that actually influence customer segmentation.

Observations:¶

  • The Income column had 24 missing values.

  • Before deciding whether to fill the missing Income values with the mean or median, I first checked if there were any extreme values (outliers) in the data. I used the interquartile range (IQR) method and found a few incomes that were much higher than the rest — some reaching over 600,000, which is far above the typical range. These large values would pull the mean upward, making it less representative of most customers. That’s why I chose to use the median instead, as it better reflects the central value without being affected by extreme outliers.

  • After replacing the missing Income values with the median, I checked the dataset’s mean income before and after filling the gaps. The mean did not change significantly, which confirmed that using the median preserved the overall distribution of the data while avoiding distortion from extreme values.

  • Mean Income (Before) : $52247.97

  • Mean Income (After) : $52237.97

Observations:¶

After removing the four columns (ID, Z_CostContact, Z_Revenue, and Dt_Customer) because they do not add significance to the analysis, I identified 182 duplicate rows in the dataset. Before removing these columns, there were no duplicates because the ID column ensured each record was unique. Now that the unique identifier is gone, the duplicates represent truly identical customer profiles. It is better to remove these 182 duplicate rows to avoid redundancy and prevent bias in the analysis results.

# Loop through numeric columns in df, plot, and add observations
for col in df.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']).columns:
    print(f"Column: {col}")

    # Calculate skew
    skew_value = round(df[col].skew(), 2)
    print(f"Skew: {skew_value}")

    # Create hist & boxplot
    plt.figure(figsize=(15, 4))

    # Histogram
    plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
    df[col].hist(bins=10, grid=False)
    plt.ylabel('Count')
    plt.title(f'Histogram of {col}')

    # Boxplot
    plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
    sns.boxplot(x=df[col])
    plt.title(f'Boxplot of {col}')

    plt.show()

    # Inference based on skewness
    if skew_value > 0.5:
        if skew_value > 1:
            print(f"Observation: {col} is highly **right-skewed** (positive skew = {skew_value}).")
            print("Possible inference: Data has a long tail to the right; a few very high values may be pulling the mean upward.")
        else:
            print(f"Observation: {col} is moderately **right-skewed** (positive skew = {skew_value}).")
            print("Possible inference: Slight concentration of lower values with some high outliers.")

    elif skew_value < -0.5:
        if skew_value < -1:
            print(f"Observation: {col} is highly **left-skewed** (negative skew = {skew_value}).")
            print("Possible inference: Data has a long tail to the left; a few very low values may be pulling the mean downward.")
        else:
            print(f"Observation: {col} is moderately **left-skewed** (negative skew = {skew_value}).")
            print("Possible inference: Slight concentration of higher values with some low outliers.")

    else:
        print(f"Observation: {col} is approximately symmetric (skew = {skew_value}).")
        print("Possible inference: Values are fairly balanced around the center.")

    print("-" * 80)

  • Overall, the skewness suggests that a few customers have significantly higher spending and income than the rest, which can impact clustering and segmentation results.

# Write your code here

# Select numeric columns with valid data
numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']).dropna(axis=1, how='all')

# Correlation matrix
corr_matrix = numeric_cols.corr()

# Heatmap
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 10))
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap='coolwarm', center=0, linewidths=0.5)
plt.title("Correlation Heatmap of Numeric Variables", fontsize=16)
plt.show()

# Pairplot (pick first 6 numeric columns to keep it readable)
sns.pairplot(numeric_cols.iloc[:, :6], diag_kind='kde')
plt.suptitle("Pairplot of Selected Numeric Variables", y=1.02)
plt.show()

# Flatten correlation matrix
corr_pairs = corr_matrix.unstack().sort_values(ascending=False)

# Filter out self-correlations
corr_pairs = corr_pairs[corr_pairs < 1]

# Top correlations (absolute > 0.5)
high_corr_pairs = corr_pairs[abs(corr_pairs) > 0.5]
print("High correlation pairs:\n", high_corr_pairs.head(10))

# Bottom correlations (absolute < 0.1)
low_corr_pairs = corr_pairs[abs(corr_pairs) < 0.1]
print("\nLow correlation pairs:\n", low_corr_pairs.head(10))

K-means Clustering¶

Question 7 : Select the appropriate number of clusters using the elbow Plot. What do you think is the appropriate number of clusters?¶

In [77]:
# Write your code here


# 1) Select numeric columns
df_numeric = df.select_dtypes(include=['number']).copy()

# 2) Scale them (IMPORTANT for K-Means)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X = scaler.fit_transform(df_numeric)   # <-- use X from here on

# 3) Elbow method on scaled data
K = range(1, 11)
wcss = []
for k in K:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init='auto')
    km.fit(X)                          # <-- use X (scaled), not df_numeric
    wcss.append(km.inertia_)

# 4) Distance-to-line heuristic to pick elbow k
ks = np.array(list(K), dtype=float)
w = np.array(wcss, dtype=float)
p1 = np.array([ks[0], w[0]])
p2 = np.array([ks[-1], w[-1]])
line_vec = p2 - p1
dist = np.abs(np.cross(line_vec, np.column_stack([ks, w]) - p1)) / np.linalg.norm(line_vec)
elbow_k = int(ks[np.argmax(dist)])

# 5) Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(ks, w, 'bo-', label='WCSS (scaled)')
plt.scatter([elbow_k], [wcss[elbow_k-1]], s=120, marker='x', color='red', label=f'Elbow k={elbow_k}')
plt.xlabel('Number of clusters (k)')
plt.ylabel('WCSS')
plt.title('Elbow Method (scaled features)')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(f"Best elbow k (distance-to-line heuristic): {elbow_k}")

Best elbow k (distance-to-line heuristic): 3
Observations:¶

Using the elbow method on the scaled dataset, the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) shows a sharp drop from k=1 to k=3, after which the rate of decrease slows noticeably. This indicates that most of the variance is explained by the first three clusters, and adding more clusters beyond this point results in diminishing returns. The distance-to-line heuristic clearly identifies k=3 as the elbow point, suggesting that the dataset naturally forms three meaningful groupings.

Key Takeaway: k=3 provides a balance between simplicity and granularity, capturing the main structure of the data while avoiding overfitting with too many clusters.

    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42)
    labels = kmeans.fit_predict(df_scaled)  # use scaled data
    silhouette_scores[k] = silhouette_score(df_scaled, labels)

# --- Plot ---

plt.xlabel('Number of clusters (k)')
plt.ylabel('Silhouette Score')
plt.title('Silhouette Score (scaled features)')
plt.show()

# --- Print sorted scores ---
print("Silhouette Scores (Highest to Lowest):")
best_k, best_score = max(silhouette_scores.items(), key=lambda x: x[1])
for k, score in sorted(silhouette_scores.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True):
    marker = " <--- Best k" if k == best_k else ""
    print(f"k = {k}: {score:.4f}{marker}")

The silhouette analysis reveals that k=2 yields the highest silhouette score (~0.264), indicating the strongest separation between clusters. This suggests that the dataset can be cleanly divided into two distinct groups with minimal overlap in feature space. As the number of clusters increases beyond k=2, the silhouette score drops, reflecting reduced cohesion within clusters and weaker separation between them.

Key Takeaway: k=2 results in the most distinct and well-separated clusters, ideal when prioritizing clear group boundaries over fine-grained segmentation.

Observation from Elbow Method (k=3):¶

Cluster 0 – Mid-Income Moderate Buyers¶

Observation

This cluster consists of customers with a median income of about 36K, typically born in the early 1970s, often with one child but no teenagers. Spending is moderate, with wines (26 median units) and meat (18 median units) as their main categories. Other product categories show low purchase volumes. They tend to visit websites more often (7 visits/month) but make relatively few store or catalog purchases.

Key Takeaway

Represents a stable mid-income segment with moderate engagement. Potential exists for upselling and cross-selling in under-purchased categories.

Cluster 1 – High-Income Heavy Spenders¶

Observation

These customers have a median income of about 69K, are typically born in the mid-1960s, and have minimal children at home. They are the highest spenders across almost all categories, especially wines (497 median units), meat (232), and gold products (45). They are highly active in store and catalog purchases and participate in campaigns at a higher rate than other clusters.

Key Takeaway

This is the core high-value customer base. Retention strategies, loyalty rewards, and premium offerings could further strengthen their lifetime value.

⸻

Cluster 2 – Ultra-High-Income Low Spenders¶

Observation

This small group has an exceptionally high median income (666K) but surprisingly low spending across all categories—wines (9), meat (18), and gold products (12). They usually have one child, no teenagers, and low purchase activity both online and in stores.

Key Takeaway

Represents an underutilized premium segment. High-income but low-spend behavior signals an opportunity for personalized marketing and exclusive offers to unlock spending potential.

Cluster 0 – Mid-Income Moderate Buyers¶

Observation

This cluster’s median income is about 36K, with members generally born in the early 1970s. Most households have one child and no teenagers. Cluster 1 – High-Income Heavy Spenders¶

Observation

This group has a median income of about 69K and members typically born in the mid-1960s. Households rarely have children but sometimes have teenagers. They are the highest spenders across nearly all categories, with particularly large purchases in wines (505 median units), meat (239), and gold products (45). They are active in store, catalog, and online purchasing channels and show higher acceptance rates for campaigns compared to Cluster 0.

Key Takeaway

Represents the premium, high-value customer base. High engagement across channels suggests strong loyalty—ideal candidates for exclusive promotions, loyalty rewards, and premium product launches to further increase spend and retention.

# Write your code here

# From the Elow we identified K = 3
k = 3
features = X_prof.columns.drop('Cluster') if 'Cluster' in X_prof.columns else X_prof.columns  # adjust if needed

# 1) (Re)fit KMeans and ensure Cluster labels exist
km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42)
labels = km.fit_predict(X_prof[features])
X_prof['Cluster'] = labels

# 2) Scale features for fair comparison in the barplot (does NOT change your original data)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled_for_plot = X_prof.copy()
X_scaled_for_plot[features] = scaler.fit_transform(X_scaled_for_plot[features])

# 3) Compute cluster means and melt for plotting
cluster_means = (
    X_scaled_for_plot.groupby('Cluster')[features]
    .mean()
    .reset_index()
    .melt(id_vars='Cluster', var_name='Feature', value_name='Mean_Value')
)

# 4) Barplot
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 7))
sns.barplot(
    data=cluster_means,
    x='Feature', y='Mean_Value',
    hue='Cluster',
    hue_order=sorted(cluster_means['Cluster'].unique())
)
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.title(f'Cluster Profiling using Barplots (k={k})')
plt.ylabel('Mean (scaled)')
plt.xlabel('Features')
plt.legend(title='Cluster')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations: K = 3¶

The three-cluster solution shows distinct feature patterns when standardized. One cluster exhibits relatively higher scaled values across multiple purchase-related features, indicating stronger customer engagement across several product categories. Another cluster displays above-average scaled scores in income-related features, suggesting a more affluent segment. The remaining cluster has generally lower scaled values across most features, pointing to a less engaged or lower-spending group.

Key Takeaways:

  • Clear separation exists between high, moderate, and low engagement segments.
  • Certain product categories stand out as potential differentiators for targeting.
  • Income differences are noticeable, but engagement patterns vary independently of income.

Business Recommedations¶

Question 12: Based on the cluster insights, what business recommendations can be provided?¶

  1. Prioritize High-Value Clusters

Focus on customers with high income and purchase activity by offering premium products, loyalty rewards, and exclusive deals. This segment has the highest immediate ROI potential.

  1. Re-Engage Low-Activity Customers

For low-engagement clusters, use targeted awareness campaigns, introductory discounts, and education about product benefits to stimulate interest and encourage first or repeat purchases.

  1. Optimize Offers by Segment

Tailor promotions to each cluster:

  • High-value: Bundle offers, early access launches.
  • Moderate-value: Cross-sell related products, subscription models.
  • Low-value: Entry-level pricing, low-commitment packages.
